   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

raw_comment:
Maggie, Hollow, Caiden, Kelly

Meddling Medals

We noticed that the different colors are for the kind of medals. The lower tiers have more lines/types of medals. We think this graph raises American egos because it shows America has the most 1st place medals by far. USA has more medals in gold, silver, and bronze. Ukraine has a higher placement than Norway, even though Norway has more gold medals.  We noticed that USA and China are the only countries that are solid colors on the graph. What are  there four axis'? 

What do the little circles on Britain and France represent? We saw that the USA and China have the same number of gold medals and that USA has more silver and bronze. Why does the graph have "Only care about gold medals" and how does it show this? We noticed that the gold medals are worth 20 times more than the silver medals. Each corner of the box for the countries have a different meaning. Smaller/less populated countries tend to value medals more equally compared to the USA and China. How could proportions of country size/population be included in this graph? We saw that the more red toned the country is the higher the ranking is. The countries are from all over the world and not one continent. We wonder why they limited the graph to only these countries, is there a significance to these countries? We noticed that the less medals they have the more divided the graph of the country is.

2.

3.

I noticed that bigger, more influential countries did better in the olympics compared to smaller countries, and those with less influence/ resources.

I wonder why China and America have the same number of gold medals, but America has so many more silver and bronze ones, even though China has a much larger population compared to America.

4. What's The Worth of Gold?
1. I notice some countries have and equal amount of gold medals but less top three's so they placed lower. If this is the case, then when really is the worth of a gold medal?
2.  I wonder if the sport that was competed in matters. I also wonder if it matters how many vicotries you've had in the past, because some countries just received their first ever gold.
3. This has little to no impact on my community as nobody I know even knows about this.

raw_comment:
1.
I noticed that US and China are tied in gold, it's interesting to see that for gold they are tied however silver and bronze both have major differences when we compare The graph also gradually decreases to the countries with the lowest amounts of medals as a whole. As it decreases, the gradients get more and more visible, leaving America to be one of the only ones with a solid color. Regardless of if we changed the values of the medals, America would still be on top considering that each category of medals have at least 40 each. 
2.
I wonder how other countries may perceive their accomplishments individually. Do some of them take bronze like how America takes Gold? Im wondering the different values each country has when it comes to each medal.
3.
This can relate to me and my community because the olympics is a huge part of America. This country does great at appreciating what each athlete does to represent us when it comes to athleticism, and these graphs show how much that pays off along with their hard work.
4.
The Truth About Medals

   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

raw_comment:
I observed that the U.S. and China were neck and neck in the Olympic medal count, tied specifically for the most important measure: gold medals. The graph illustrates the gradual shifts in rankings, with each country either climbing or slipping over time. If we were to give equal weight to bronze medals as we do to gold, the U.S. would still hold the top spot. However, doing so would allow several other nations would rise in the rankings. I also noticed how the graph used color gradients for all countries except the U.S. and China, where a warmer, darker tone represented a closer position to first place. Cooler, lighter tones reflected a lower standing. As the ranking decreases, the complexity of their graph increases.

I’m curious about how the various countries perceive their Olympic achievements separately. Do they place more importance on winning gold, or do they honor all medals with equal pride? How does such a perception differ from country to country? 

This connects with my own community, where many aspiring athletes dream of achieving similar success on a global stage. The Olympics have become not just a showcase of talent but a symbol of national pride, particularly for the United States, which continues to lead in the medal counts.

Going for Gold: Do Medals Really Matter?

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

Thanks to all the students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received: 

“How the Value of Gold, Silver and Bronze Reshapes Olympic Leaderboards” by Alessandro of Wantagh, N.Y., 
“Who Really Won the Olympics? Reevaluating Medal Counts” by Henry of Andover High School in Mass.,
“Should We Meddle with the Value of the Medals?” by Noah from Gull Lake High School in Richland, Mich., 
“Quality or Quantity: How Valuing Medals Changes the Ranks of Olympic Competing Countries" by Layla from Gull Lake High School in Richland, Mich.
"One team's fourth is another team's tenth: Olympic scoring could affect how your country places in future games." by Emma of Cambria High School
"Medal Math: Does Gold Shine Brighter Than Silver and Bronze?" from Jayden of Perth Amboy High School 

Please return on Friday when we will reveal the free link to the article that included this graph, a summary of the article, additional questions, shout outs for some of the best headlines for the graph and Stat Nuggets -- definitions of words that relate to the graphs and where you can find them in the graphs. 

The next graph will be released by Friday, September 20.  The topic – hot Las Vegas.  

Signing off – Sharon Hessney from Boston, who watched in awe for the first time the sport climbing, rhythmic gymnastics and breaking, and Chris Luzniak of Columbus, Ohio, who watched every game of the men's and women's soccer events!

1. **Chart type**:  
   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

Because the US is first in medals in general, I wonder if there's something different about American athletes that gives them a leg up when it comes to the Olympics. Perhaps it's the size of the US population. I know personally how much people care about the Olympics here in America, so maybe that's an incentive. As an American, I enjoy seeing how well my country does in the Olympics, and it's great way of showing patriotism. Title: "USA on top"

raw_comment:
Initially, I notice that the graphs are ranked highest to lowest in the countries with the most medals overall. However, while analyzing the graphs I see that the further down you go, the more discrepancies there are within them. For instance, the U.S. has the most medals overall, but is also tied with China for gold medals. Yet, China is ranked lower since they have less medals than the U.S. Using this knowledge, it appears that the graphs seem to emphasize the importance of the different medals. For example, Great Britain comes in 3rd place for most medals overall, but when taking only gold medals into account they bump down to 7th place. This remains truthful throughout the graph, letting the audience know that it is not just about the medals, but the overall value they have.
I wonder if how we rank them affects how the athletes get compensation for the medals? Do countries value gold medals over silver or bronze due to the profit it may bring in? Does valuing the gold medal over silver or bronze diminish the hard work of the other athletes?
The way we value one athlete's accomplishments over the other relates to my community and country. In society, we recognize and value the athlete with the highest accomplishment, but that does not diminish the other awards as well. It is easy to get wrapped up in the numbers, being first overall, however that should not take away from someone who received second or lower.
"Who's on top of the pyramid: Gold, Silver, or Bronze?"

   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

raw_comment:
1. The graph shows that different methods of valuing Olympic medals can lead to significantly different rankings of countries. For example, while the United States consistently ranks high regardless of how medals are valued, Brazil's rank changes drastically depending on whether bronze medals are valued equally with gold and silver or not.

2. I wonder how different countries value their own achievements in the Olympics. Do they prioritize gold medals over silver and bronze, or do they celebrate all victories equally? Additionally, how do these values influence the athletes' motivation?

3. In my community, we often celebrate local athletes and their accomplishments. This graph shows the importance of recognizing achievements differently based on context. In our local sports events, while winning might be the primary focus, the effort and participation of all athletes should also be celebrated.

4. "Medal Math: Does Gold Shine Brighter Than Silver and Bronze?"

raw_comment:
1. What do you notice? 
I noticed that this graph is showing different countries' rankings or positions based on which country won the most gold medals during the 2024 Summer olympics. The United States and China are both tied with an equal amount of gold medals. These rankings are separated in what I can physically see, a rainbow order. I’ve come to the conclusion that they are color coordinated to indicate who won first to last. Since the United States came in first place with the larger amount of gold medals, it was given the color red: The first color of the rainbow. The different shades of blue, green and purple are used to represent the different numerical positions as shown on the image. 

2. What do you wonder?
If China placed 3rd to 7th but France placed 3rd to 5th, why does China come in before France? Was it purposely placed like this? Is it trying to show/indicate something? 

3. How does this relate to your community?
It doesn’t necessarily relate to my community or region in specific, but to everyone that lives in the United States. Our country placed first place with the most gold medals, representing and helping the United States gain more recognition around the globe, yet again. 

4. Title
United States vs. China: Who will lead in the next four years?
United States: More gold to represent.

I also notice that some countries that are struggling or going through war are doing better than some countries that aren’t struggling. I notice that the U.S. and China did extremely well in the Olympics, and both had the most Gold medals. The graph is showing each of the countries progress, going up or down in its place. If we only measured bronze medals just as gold, then the US would still be the most successful but the other countries would progress and move to a higher ranking. 

I wonder how some countries are still winning medals, when their countries are dealing with crisis and various problems. How do these athletes get the proper training and materials if there countries are in a crisis (ex: Ukraine). 

This relates to my community because US did the best in the Olympics, so it is reflecting our success and the handwork our country did to train these athletes to do so well. This does not really relate to me personally, because I did not watch the Olympics this year.

   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed the different colors for each medal that the country had won.
The United States has the most medals in bronze and silver. 
Both China and the United States have the same amount of gold medals. 
Jamaica has the least gold, bronze, and silver medals. 

 What do you wonder?
Why is Britain in third place, but has the least amount of medals compared to France?
What do the lines mean, when the country has the same number?
How come out of all the countries that competed in the Olympics only these ten were graphed? 

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because it shows how our country is doing in the Olympics. It always gives those who want to compete to have more motivation. 

What’s going on in this graph?
Chasing After the Gold

   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

Meddling Medals

Each corner of the box for the countries have a different meaning. Smaller/less populated countries tend to value medals more equally compared to the USA and China. How could proportions of country size/population be included in this graph? We saw that the more red toned the country is the higher the ranking is. The countries are from all over the world and not one continent. We wonder why they limited the graph to only these countries, is there a significance to these countries? We noticed that the less medals they have the more divided the graph of the country is.

1. 
I have noticed that as the graphs descend, the colors become more of a cool tone, and they get progressively more complex. for example, the United States graph is completely dark red with no white lines, but the Jamaica graph is navy blue and has a lot more lines that look like a landscape. It also seems that the top two rows (US to Canada) are all warm colors. On only the bottom row there are cool colors.
2.
I wonder if the graphs other than the United States have the same numbers or if they are completely different. Since it only shoes numbers for the United States, there are not many ways to know what the others are.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

raw_comment:
I noticed that bigger, more influential countries did better in the olympics compared to smaller countries, and those with less influence/ resources.

I wonder why China and America have the same number of gold medals, but America has so many more silver and bronze ones, even though China has a much larger population compared to America.

This relates to me because I am a U.S. citizen, and just as a person in this world because it is a worldwide event.

The headline I choose for this graph is "The Race For Third Place" because I wanted to highlight how immovable America and China are in their respective first and second place spots in the olympics, and how the only chance any other country has is to be third.

   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|

| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

raw_comment:
'Does the style of medal or the amount of medals determine the rank of country?'

1. While looking at these graphs I noticed that China and the US are tied in gold medals but way different numbers in medal and bronze. It's kind of confusing how each place can have the same amount of gold medals but very different amounts of bronze and silver. I think this might be due to the different amount of people in the Olympics of each place.    
2. I also noticed how because the US have more medals overall they are in first place.
3. This goes along with smaller places as well. for example Kenya has four gold medals while Ukraine has three. But Ukraine is still ranked above.

So if the quantity of medals in a country determine what place they are in why does it matter what color medal you got? I believe in this case they should all count the same.

|---|---|---|

| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

raw_comment:
I observed that the U.S. and China were neck and neck in the Olympic medal count, tied specifically for the most important measure: gold medals. The graph illustrates the gradual shifts in rankings, with each country either climbing or slipping over time. If we were to give equal weight to bronze medals as we do to gold, the U.S. would still hold the top spot. However, doing so would allow several other nations would rise in the rankings. I also noticed how the graph used color gradients for all countries except the U.S. and China, where a warmer, darker tone represented a closer position to first place. Cooler, lighter tones reflected a lower standing. As the ranking decreases, the complexity of their graph increases.

I’m curious about how the various countries perceive their Olympic achievements separately. Do they place more importance on winning gold, or do they honor all medals with equal pride? How does such a perception differ from country to country? 

This connects with my own community, where many aspiring athletes dream of achieving similar success on a global stage. The Olympics have become not just a showcase of talent but a symbol of national pride, particularly for the United States, which continues to lead in the medal counts.

Going for Gold: Do Medals Really Matter?

raw_comment:
Thanks to all the students who responded.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received: 

“How the Value of Gold, Silver and Bronze Reshapes Olympic Leaderboards” by Alessandro of Wantagh, N.Y., 
“Who Really Won the Olympics? Reevaluating Medal Counts” by Henry of Andover High School in Mass.,
“Should We Meddle with the Value of the Medals?” by Noah from Gull Lake High School in Richland, Mich., 
“Quality or Quantity: How Valuing Medals Changes the Ranks of Olympic Competing Countries" by Layla from Gull Lake High School in Richland, Mich.
"One team's fourth is another team's tenth: Olympic scoring could affect how your country places in future games." by Emma of Cambria High School
"Medal Math: Does Gold Shine Brighter Than Silver and Bronze?" from Jayden of Perth Amboy High School 

Please return on Friday when we will reveal the free link to the article that included this graph, a summary of the article, additional questions, shout outs for some of the best headlines for the graph and Stat Nuggets -- definitions of words that relate to the graphs and where you can find them in the graphs. 

The next graph will be released by Friday, September 20.  The topic – hot Las Vegas.  

Signing off – Sharon Hessney from Boston, who watched in awe for the first time the sport climbing, rhythmic gymnastics and breaking, and Chris Luzniak of Columbus, Ohio, who watched every game of the men's and women's soccer events!

   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

raw_comment: I noticed that the US and China are tied regarding gold medals. I found it interesting that China and the United States were both first and second all across the board, while others (such as Britain) were third place while counting all medals equally but seventh when only counting gold medals. The difference between China and Britain's gold medals is so significant, and it makes me wonder what puts China and America so far ahead. I wonder if there are specific aspects that make one country more likely to win medals than others. Because the US is first in medals in general, I wonder if there's something different about American athletes that gives them a leg up when it comes to the Olympics. Perhaps it's the size of the US population. I know personally how much people care about the Olympics here in America, so maybe that's an incentive. As an American, I enjoy seeing how well my country does in the Olympics, and it's great way of showing patriotism. Title: "USA on top"

raw_comment:
Initially, I notice that the graphs are ranked highest to lowest in the countries with the most medals overall. However, while analyzing the graphs I see that the further down you go, the more discrepancies there are within them. For instance, the U.S. has the most medals overall, but is also tied with China for gold medals. Yet, China is ranked lower since they have less medals than the U.S. Using this knowledge, it appears that the graphs seem to emphasize the importance of the different medals. For example, Great Britain comes in 3rd place for most medals overall, but when taking only gold medals into account they bump down to 7th place. This remains truthful throughout the graph, letting the audience know that it is not just about the medals, but the overall value they have.
I wonder if how we rank them affects how the athletes get compensation for the medals? Do countries value gold medals over silver or bronze due to the profit it may bring in? Does valuing the gold medal over silver or bronze diminish the hard work of the other athletes?
The way we value one athlete's accomplishments over the other relates to my community and country. In society, we recognize and value the athlete with the highest accomplishment, but that does not diminish the other awards as well. It is easy to get wrapped up in the numbers, being first overall, however that should not take away from someone who received second or lower.
"Who's on top of the pyramid: Gold, Silver, or Bronze?"

1. What do you notice? 
I noticed that this graph is showing different countries' rankings or positions based on which country won the most gold medals during the 2024 Summer olympics. The United States and China are both tied with an equal amount of gold medals. These rankings are separated in what I can physically see, a rainbow order. I’ve come to the conclusion that they are color coordinated to indicate who won first to last. Since the United States came in first place with the larger amount of gold medals, it was given the color red: The first color of the rainbow. The different shades of blue, green and purple are used to represent the different numerical positions as shown on the image. 

2. What do you wonder?
If China placed 3rd to 7th but France placed 3rd to 5th, why does China come in before France? Was it purposely placed like this? Is it trying to show/indicate something? 

3. How does this relate to your community?
It doesn’t necessarily relate to my community or region in specific, but to everyone that lives in the United States. Our country placed first place with the most gold medals, representing and helping the United States gain more recognition around the globe, yet again. 

4. Title
United States vs. China: Who will lead in the next four years?
United States: More gold to represent.

raw_comment:
1) What I noticed is that the different countries are placed differently depending on how they score. I also notice that some countries that are struggling or going through war are doing better than some countries that aren’t struggling. I noticed that China and The United States won 40 gold medals and Britain and France, who are in third place, only received 13 gold medals which is a very big difference. Finally, I also noticed that places 1 all the way to 24 are in different colors/shades.

2)  I wonder why this is even a thing. Why are countries prioritizing their medal counts or the material of them and whether that affects the way they play and their strategies? Why do medal counts and colors determine if you are doing a great job? I also wonder what the black circles on some of the graphs mean and why these specific colors were picked. Is there a hidden message behind them that we should be aware of? 

3) This relates to my community because this graph shows how the United States is doing in the Olympics and it also shows if they are having good strategies. On the other hand, it has a very small impact on me because I don’t really enjoy sports therefore, I don’t usually watch it or judge it. 

4) Does The Material, Color and Count of Medals Really Determine How Good You Are?

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.
raw_comment:
​​1. What do you notice?

- Countries rankings change based on how medals are valued. The U.S. and China stay on top, but countries like Brazil drop when gold and silver medals are weighted more.

2. What do you wonder?

- I wonder how other country's rankings would change if different medal values were applied. How would smaller countries compare if we looked at medals per person?

3. How does this relate to you and your community?

- It shows that how we define success can depend on what we value

4. Catchy headline:  
-“Gold vs Total”: The Olympics Ranks Worth

raw_comment:
I notice that the U.S. and China did extremely well in the Olympics, and both had the most Gold medals. The graph is showing each of the countries progress, going up or down in its place. If we only measured bronze medals just as gold, then the US would still be the most successful but the other countries would progress and move to a higher ranking. 

I wonder how some countries are still winning medals, when their countries are dealing with crisis and various problems. How do these athletes get the proper training and materials if there countries are in a crisis (ex: Ukraine). 

This relates to my community because US did the best in the Olympics, so it is reflecting our success and the handwork our country did to train these athletes to do so well. This does not really relate to me personally, because I did not watch the Olympics this year.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.
raw_comment: After analyzing the graphs above, it becomes evident that the ranking of countries in the medal count can vary based on how the medals are valued. It's intriguing to observe how different countries' performances can shift based on the method of counting medals and assigning values to gold, silver, and bronze. For instance, nations that dominate in silver and bronze medals might experience significant shifts in their rankings depending on how much they prioritize gold medals. The United States consistently excels across all ranking criteria, whereas countries like Brazil witness substantial fluctuations in their positions based on the significance attributed to various medals. I wonder how countries prioritize their medal counts and whether it affects their overall Olympic strategies. This relates to me and my community as it shows that the value placed on different types of medals can significantly impact the final rankings of countries. Headline: "Medal Count Madness”

raw_comment: I notice that both the United States and China are tied with 40 gold medals, having far more gold medals than the other countries.  Although the United States and China are tied for gold medals, the United States has significantly more silver and bronze medals than China.  I also notice the use of color to demonstrate the scale of 1st-25th or lower.  I wonder if the United States, China, Britain, and France are red or orange because they are closer to 1st, being "warmer," while Jamaica is blue because it is farthest from 1st, or "cooler."  I thought it was very interesting that they used colors to depict the colors and rankings of the Olympic medals won by each country.  This relates to me and my community because the United States came in first, and as a citizen of the United States, I am proud of the American Olympians who made this achievement possible.  I watched many of the athletes win their gold, silver, and bronze medals from home with my family and friends, and the Olympic milestones that were achieved in the 2024 games gave the United States and its citizens a sense of pride.  A catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea is, "Hot or Cold: 2024 Olympic Winnings"

   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.

   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |

| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.
raw_comment:
I noticed that the US and China are tied for 40 gold medals and then Britain/France, who are in third place, only received 13 gold medals which is a huge discrepancy. I also noticed that places 1-24 are all denoted by different shades/colors. However, I wonder why places 25-46 are all denoted by the same shade of blue. This relates to me and my community because living in the United States, having won such a competitive competition makes me and my country feel a great sense of pride. Because of this, we all feel a sense of unity as a country when we at times are divided.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.
raw_comment:
What do you notice? If your notice makes a claim, where in the graph is the evidence to support it?

I notice that as the numbers get lower and lower in place, the graphs become more and more complex. For example, Great Britain only has 3 sections (from 3rd to potentially 7th) while Jamaica’s rankings vary from 33rd to 46th place.

What do you wonder?

I wonder about which medals matter more, and if a large number of bronze and silver medals could overtake a country that has only a few gold medals.

What impact does this have on you and your community?

This has a very small impact on my local community of Andover/Massachusetts, but my country (the United States) was the leader in all aspects, whether the medal count was weighted differently or not.

What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.

One is Silver and the Other is Gold: How the Medal Counts of the Olympics Compare

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.
raw_comment:
1. I noticed that there are countries with an equal number of gold medals, but are not equally represented. For example, China's graph is not accurately portrayed because although both China and the United States earned 40 gold medals, the top right corner of China's data is colored in a lighter shade of red than the top right corner of the United States' data. Additionally, all of China's factors are ranked in 2nd place, disregarding the total number of gold medals. Furthermore, this happens similarly to Italy and Germany's graphs.

I observe that each region of a country's graph has at least one ranking depending on each of the factors. The different colors in each graph denote the value of a ranking. If a country has more than one ranking in a certain area, a line separates the boundary from two or more rankings.

2.  I wonder why rankings from 25th and after are represented with the same color on the graph. For example, Norway's ranking for the category: silver medals are worth 20 times bronze medals, falls in 25th place towards the bottom half. This is denoted in blue. However, Norway's ranking for all medals of the same worth falls in 26th place represented with the same shade of blue.

3. Living in the United States, me and my community can acknowledge and be proud of our country's achievements.

4. The 2024 Olympics: Every Medal Counts

raw_comment:
I observed that the U.S. and China led the Olympic race, tying in the number of gold medals; but the US received a greater total medal count. The graph illustrates the rise or fall of each country's position. If bronze medals were weighted equally with gold, the U.S. would still remain at the top, but other countries would change in ranking. All graphs, except for those of China and the U.S., displayed color variations based on closeness to first place—the closer a country was to the top, the darker and warmer the color; the farther, the lighter and cooler the tone.

I wonder why these countries were chosen. What made these countries with lower medal count be chosen to be included in the graph. Were they just chosen at random? Or chosen to represent a specific population?

This connects with my community through the athletes at my school who dream of reaching such heights in their sports careers. The Olympics have become a source of patriotism, particularly for the U.S., which helps solidify our presence on the Olympic podium.

United States, The World Champions, no matter which way you count the medals

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the higher a country's overall place, the warmer its graph is, and the lower a country's overall place, the cooler its graph is. For example, America and China, which came in first and second overall respectively, have graphs that are dark red, whereas the graph for Jamaica, which came in between 33rd and and 46th, is a deep blue.

2. I wonder what the black circles in the US, Britain, and France graphs mean. It is unclear what their purpose is or even if they're really supposed to be there.

3. This graph makes me (and probably other Americans as well) feel good because it very clearly puts the US on top.

4. Who Really Won the Olympics? Reevaluating Medal Counts

raw_comment:
1. I notice that The United States came in first place with the most amount of medals, and China was close behind in second. Both countries had the same amount of gold medals but different amounts of silver and bronze. I also noticed that countries like Great Britain and France were ranked, but their positions change depending on how silver and bronze medals are counted.  

2. I wonder why these specific countries were picked as they seem to be relatively random towards the bottom. Also why does the graph skip from France to Canada becuase of the large difference in their scores. I also wonder if the scoring methods will change over the coming years.

3. As an american living in the United States I am proud that our country "won" the olympics and won the most amount of medals. Also over the summer I spent a lot of time watching the olympics and cheering on american athletes. The olympics unifies our country as we are all rooting for the same team.

4. Gold, Silver, Bronze, or bust?

raw_comment:
In this graph, the medal count of each country in the 2024 Paris Olympic games is shown. I notice that the USA and China were tied with gold medals, but the US had more overall medals, so they were the official winner in medal count. Many of the smaller graphs also show the difference in medal rank that countries would have if the rankings were judged in different ways. For example, Great Britain could either be 3rd or 7th in the world because they came third in overall medals and 7th in only gold medals. I wonder what specific system of ranking each individual country uses to decide which countries accomplished the most in the Olympics. It is a huge accomplishment for The United States to say that they were the undisputed winners of the Olympics. Each community in the US should take pride in that.

raw_comment:
Could the Olympic Ranking of Countries be Wrong? 

I notice that these graphs are displaying the different Olympic medal counts and the rankings. I also notice some are 100% in their ranking while others like Norway and Jamaica are extremely ranged in the possible medal ranking. For example, America is 100% first place whereas Jamaica ranges from 33rd to 46th place. I wonder why France and Britain could both be 3rd place. I think the question of how much each medal place should be worth is what is going on in this graph. I think France should easily be 3rd place and not possibly tied with Britain. France has more gold medals and silver medals than Britain. Although Britain has more bronze medals I don't think it should outweigh the factors of the gold and silver medals. I think the gold medal should be 60% value, silver should be 30% value, and bronze should only be 10% value. This relates to my community because I know that a lot of people in my community are extremely involved and passionate about the Olympics. If America was not fairly represented, I know my community would be very upset about it which makes the importance of equal representation so important in other countries as well.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that the United States and China would still be one and two no matter the value of the medals. I can see this in their graphs in which they are the same color throughout. It gets more complicated as you look at more countries, such as Britain, where they could have had five outcomes. It looks like you can choose around sixteen different outcomes for Norway’s medal count and each will give you a place between 18 and 26. The countries that had lower medal counts or finished in lower overall places had more possibilities of finishing place. I also noticed the differences in colors in the graphs(the colors decrease in “warmth” as they decrease placement). The graphs show just how complex the medal system in the Olympics is.
2. I wonder why the graphs change so much as you decrease the overall place the countries got. For example, Britain is pretty straightforward, and the wavey form it shows continues for a couple of countries, but then by the time you get to Norway and Jamaica, the graphs are a mess. Why would the shapes of the distributions change when the same conditions and rules are followed for each graph? 
3. For the United States, this graph shows dominance in the Olympics. The fact that the United States would have been first whichever way you count the medals shows the large margin of victory. This increases my pride in the United States and inspires me to root for the United States. 
4. “Did Britain or France get bronze in the Olympics? We don’t know.”

   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that when comparing the graphs, I found two countries that placed durastlicly different based on how the medals were valued.  Britain and Kenya appear to display clear, opposing results depending on the value of the medals. For example, if all medals were valued equally, this would be good news for Britain, but bad news for Kenya. raw_comment:
1. I notice that the country with the most medals overall has only 1 part. Then the third place country has 5 parts. This leads me to believe that the better a country did overall the fewer parts their graph is split into. The places also go from red to yellow to green to blue the lower the place is. The places near the bottom have much cooler colors than the places at the top.

2. I wonder if the colors picked have specific significance and or correlate with any of the medals. I wonder if the color wheel was just used to place countries in certain rankings using colors to display that.

3. This relates to my community because I am an American and it is inspiring to see that America has done the best overall. I think this is especially important to my friends and other student athletes who now can feel motivated knowing that the US can do amazing things.

4. Olympic Gold Rush

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.
raw_comment:
1. I noticed that the U.S. and China dominated the Olympic race and were tied by Gold medals. The graph shows each country's progress slowly making its way up or down in its place. If we were to measure only bronze just as gold the US would continue to be on top but other countries would move to a higher stance. All graphs except China and the US had a color variation based on how close they were to 1, the closer to 1 the darker/warmer tone of color was presented, and the farther, a cooler lighter tone. 
2. The graphs reflect how the country made its way to its place, and why the countries that didn't make it to the top 10 or 20 constantly struggled more than others to maintain their place. I believe this has something to do with countries that lack resources in sports, the socioeconomic status of the country, the compensation for winning a medal, and how aware a country's community is of the Olympic games and the impact it would have on an athlete and their country. 
3. This relates to my community through aspiring athletes who hope to one day reach such success in their athletic careers. The Olympics have become part of a country's pride, especially the U.S. which helps maintain our stance on the podium of Olympic Medals. 
4. The US dominates the Olympic Games as other Countries struggle to keep up.

1. Canada and France’s rankings don’t vary all that much even with different values appointed to the different medals, but countries like Norway and Jamaica vary greatly depending on the medal values.
2. What do the black circles represent on the graphs of Britain and France? Are they meant to be there? If so, why aren’t they on any of the other graphs? Does having fewer total medals make the change in values more impactful?

I also know that many people in my community take an interest in the ranking of countries their parents or grandparents are from, so it’s interesting to see how it can vary so greatly.

What do you notice?
	I noticed that when there are more overlaps and sections intertwining in the graph the lower that country is ranked. Also noticed that the values of the metals will affect where the countries are ranked at the end.

What do you wonder?
	I wonder why we haven’t come up with a better system that would not make people question the value of the metals. When was this decided? Who came up with the idea that gold medals are worth 20x silver. This might be discouraging and portray the idea that olympians who don’t take gold are valued less than that of gold. 

How does this relate to you and your community?

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that the U.S. and China would still be one and two no matter the value of the medals. It gets more complicated as you look at more countries, such as Britain, where they could have had five outcomes. When I look at Norway, I have very little understanding of what is going on. It looks like you can choose around sixteen different outcomes for Norway’s medal count and each will give you a place between 18 and 26. The countries that had lower medal counts or finished in lower overall places had more possibilities in finishing place when you account for all of the options they did in these graphs. I also noticed the differences in colors in the graphs. The colors decrease in “warmth” as they decrease placement. The graph shows you just how complex this medal-counting system can be.
2. I wonder why the graphs change so much as you decrease the overall place the countries got. For example, Britain is pretty straightforward, and the wavey form it shows continues for a couple of countries, but then by the time you get to Norway and Jamaica, the graphs are a mess. 
3. The graphs show the U.S. dominates the Olympics. The fact that the United States would have been first whichever way you count the medals shows the large margin of victory. This increases my pride in the United States and makes me realize the level of athletics we bring to the Olympics.
4. “Did Britain or France get bronze in the Olympics? We don’t know.”

1. **Chart type**:  
   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.
raw_comment:
What do you notice?:
- I notice that the graphs' color base is similar to a rainbow, the less you place the lower your color is on a rainbow for example, the USA was first overall no matter the value of the medal so they are always going to be red (top of the rainbow), but a country like Jamaica didn't have many medals so their place varies on the value of the medal so they were dark blue (bottom of the rainbow). I also noticed the countries with more bronze and silver medals compared to gold, have more lines on their graph because of how much their place varies when the value of the medals changes (this theory is rocky when either the country has no gold medals or has double digit medals in all 3 places). Also, for example, Jamaica again says they place anywhere from 33rd to 46th but only show the 6 places (varies depending on the country) they mostly averaged in.
What do you wonder?:
- If the medals were all equal, would participants try less because first isn't as valuable as before?  
-why choose those 10 countries to use as an example?
How does this relate to you and your community?:
-this has no impact on my community or anyone I know. People I know aren't very patriotic or celebrate the Olympics as I see online, I'm sure there are people who sit by the screen every 2 years and root for their country with pride, that isn't something I'm used to. 
Create a catchy headline:
-No gold, silver, or bronze—only a rainbow of Olympic accomplishments

raw_comment:
1) What do I notice? I notice that, as the country is ranked lower, the colors in the graph become cooler. I also noticed that the countries shown would all rank lower if the medals had equal value. Also, the United States and China are noticeably blank compared to the other countries because they would not change their rankings.
2) What do I wonder? I wonder what countries would replace the third-ranked country if the method for counting medals switched. I also wonder if people would pay more attention to countries with numerous bronze medals but little to no gold medals if that happens.  Gold medals are the most valued, and therefore the most recognized for determining a country’s skill, while bronze medals are valued more to show a country’s potential to achieve gold. I also wonder about how to decipher Norway’s and Jamaica’s graphs. 
3) How does this relate to me and my community? The Olympics are a chance for my community and me to show patriotism to the United States and cheer on athletes from our specific region. The United States also being the top-ranked country gives hope to those in my community to have a realistic chance at becoming an Olympian one day.  
4) Headline: New Olympic Ranking System: Is Gold All That Different from Silver and Bronze?

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

What do you notice?

I noticed that America came in first place and the color of the graph was a solid red. China came in second and also featured a solid red graph. The graphs from then on continued in order of the rainbow, often featuring multiple colors in a graph at once.

What do you wonder?

I wonder if the color of the graph had any relation to the information shown. I also wonder about the purpose of this graph format and why this format was chosen.

How does this relate to you and your community?

This graph gives us and our community a sense of pride as Americans and informs us of world events. 

Headline

"Stats of the Olympics"

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that the USA won the most gold medals in the 2024 Olympics out of all the countries that participated. This is all that counts for the ranking, but other things are also being graphed. Each corner of the graph has a different category determining that area’s ranking (gold worth 20x silver, gold medals, all medals valued equally, and silver worth 20x bronze). I noticed that Jamaica’s graph has multiple rankings ranging from 33rd to 46th place. 

What do you wonder?
I wonder why the map of Jamaica has so many different sections divided by lines. I also wonder what the color of the graphs has to do with the information that is displayed on them. Is there significance to the coloration?

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because the United States is part of my community, and the 2024 Olympics recently happened over the summer. The US competed as one nation in the competition, and because of our joint goal of winning, a wave of patriotism spread across the country and unified all our viewers.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.
