raw_comment:
What Do I Notice?: I noticed the graphs go from a very dark hue of red to represent the countries with the highest places in their wins, and the countries with the lowest ranks in their wins go all the way down to a dark hue of blue. The colors of the graphs basically go in the order of a rainbow, with the United States being at the very top with an entire graph full of dark red, and Jamaica being represented as the lowest ranked here with all of the darkest blue. Since all medals are being calculated as equal here, and the United States have the most medals overall, it makes sense they would be 1st. I also noticed that the multiple countries could have the same ranking places included in their graphs. 
What Do I Wonder?: I wonder why the creator of the graphs chose to use those specific colors and make them go in order of the rainbow. Why were these specific countries chosen for these graphs if there are 90 countries in total that won medals in the Olympics?
How Does This Relate to Me and My Community?: My community is so diverse with people from many countries, just as the Olympics is populated with many unique people. People in my own town try to stay very updated on the Olympics, and would cheer on their own country if they're performing in the Olympics. 
HEADLINE: "Rainbow of Nations: Diverse Olympic Medal Winners Shine Bright in Historic Games"

raw_comment:
- I notice how despite the wide range of medal merit multipliers, from 1.5 all the way 20, both the United States and China remain in first and second place, respectively, regardless of medal worth.  Additionally, the rankings of the next few countries graphed in the article fluctuate only slightly when medal worth is altered. - I wonder why the ruling and point tallying for medals in the olympics hasn’t been set in stone yet. It feels like one of, if not the most, integral parts of score keeping, and should be ironed out and upheld so as to keep the games fair for competitors.

- interesting headline: in for a penny, in for a pound: the notoriously skewed olympic scoring system is being reconsidered.

   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

1. **Chart type**:  
   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the U.S and China would get the same places no matter the value system used, but places like Britain would be placed in a different way. I also notice that the places in red only care about gold medals. U.S and China both got 40 gold medals, so the judges had to use the silver medal count to determine a winner. I wonder why gold medals count more then all medals combined. It asks the question what is the point of having silver and bronze medals if they are not valued. I also wonder what the lines on the Jamaica graph mean. It is all one color but all split up. 
Olympics are a big deal not just in my community, but all around the world. For such an exciting event, how should know how the actual scoring works. My headline would be  "How does Olympic scoring work?".

raw_comment:
What do I notice?
I noticed how the USA is far ahead in the total olympic medal count. However, China and the USA are both tied at 40 gold medals. The graph is showing the 10 countries from the summer olympics. I noticed that as the countries medals decreased, the colors of the countries went “down” the rainbow (first red, next orange, then yellow, and so on). 

What do you wonder?
I wonder why these 10 specific countries were picked. I also wonder if the world will ever have a universal way to determine a winner. Another thing I wonder is what the lines on the graphs mean. 

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to most US citizens because the US is almost always the leader in the gold medal aspect. For the US, it has always been easy to say we are the winners of the olympics due to us obtaining the most gold medals and overall medals. However, with the US and China tying in the gold medal category, questions have been raised whether we can declare the US as an overall winner. Overall, this relates to my community because there are now questions raised about whether or not the winner of the olympics should be determined by total medals or gold medals.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice that no matter how you count the medals the US and China stay on top. I also noticed that many countries would benefit from all the medals equalling the same point value. 
What do you wonder?
I wonder what country would come out on top when population is put into consideration. The US and China are both very populated countries and send many athletes but some countries only send a handful because their population is much smaller. So would a smaller country come out on top when the ratio of medals is compared with population?
How does this relate to you and your community?
Concerning this graph, my community is America. The USA comes out on top in all the common scoring methods. The outcome of the Olympic games changes people's view of America. So even though we would win no matter what it's important to choose a good scoring method to show that we not only won but deserved it. Also, this method can be used in future years to determine the winner, which might be America again. 
Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.
Is Bronze the New Gold?

I notice how much the place that a country gets in the olympics significantly changes based on what medals are counted and how each is valued towards a countries final score.
What do I wonder?
I wonder why the Olympics use the primary gold medal tally that they do currently. This system lessens the value of silver and especially bronze medals even though it is a major accomplishment to achieve one.
How does this relate to you and your community?
To the United States, for most of the Olympics before tying with China we had less gold medals than they did, but almost double the amounts of silver and bronze medals. If we had one less gold medal, we would have come second in the olympics despite having the most number of total, bronze, and silver medals by far.

Headline: “Medals Don’t Matter? Why the Olympics Medal Tally Deincentivises Silver and Bronze Medals”

sentence_classifications.image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

raw_comment:
a)What do you notice?
After examining the graph, it portrays what medals each country has won. There are different values given to each medal. The United States was clearing first place in all ways because of the large amount of gold medals. China was second. As rankings went down, so did the brightness of the color. I wonder what impacted the rankings the most. Its also interesting how the different medals still had the same value as some of the gold, like the bronze.
b) What do you wonder?
I wonder what impacted the rankings the most and how everything is decided. I want to know who is considered third place, since the graph doesn’t showcase that. I want to know why the colors dim down as we go farther down the pyramid. 
c) How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me and my community because it's really cool to see how the actual scores and medals get decided. It relates to my community because I love the United States and our country has won the most. 
d) Catchy headline:
"Does the medal matter?"

raw_comment:
1. When I look at this graph, I notice how the farther down the leader board you travel, the more diverse the placing is for each listed team.  The US and China are clearly on the podium, but every other country, in moderation, is liable to receive a differing place in scoring.  

2.  What I wonder is how the majority of the countries that participate in the Olympics score themselves.  Is there a sort of universal understanding of who takes what place in the world stage of athletics, or is this a highly debated topic for most other countries around the world?  Cool to think about.

3.  Clearly, I live in the  United States of America, so I don't have much of an argument in mind for my country's own success within the Olympic games.  As for myself and my community, our country got a win over everybody else's countries, so that acts as a slight boost to our national morale.  But on the other hand, my mind goes to the idea of countries who don't really appreciate each other (for example : The USA and China) being pushed into even further odds from each other.  I'm not saying that the Olympics would cause the USA and China to go to war, but I can't see us metaphorically dunking on them helping to strengthen international ties in any sort of way.    A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

I notice that the US and China got first and second no matter how they are weighed but some of the other countries could be placed way differently based on what system is used. Like Britain could be in 3rd place through 7th and Jamaica could be from 33th to 46th place.

raw_comment:
1. This graph is showing how different countries compared when looking at the amount of medals each country won. The different colors are showing how the country would have placed when treated the medals differently based on color. The US placed first no matter how you count the medals and China placed second no matter what. The colors seem to get lighter as the placing goes down. These charts seem to be depicted over one another because it is showing ranking.I think it would be best to count medals differently by color because they are different achievements, so they shouldn't be counted the same. 
2.  I wonder why these specific countries were picked. It seems to be at random, but I wonder if there was more thought there than what it seems. I want to know why some of the countries are split up into so many different sections with different placings, but the whole box is still just one color. Was there a more efficient way to show this data? Could it have been conveyed more clearly? 
3. This relates to my community because it is always exciting to see how the Olympics play out, but confusing when the final rankings come out. This is because of the discrepancy of if all medals should count the same. This graph displays how different ranks can be depending on how medals are counted. Hopefully this can be used to fix the problem that comes with deciding the "winners" of the Olympics. 
4. I would title this graph: Medals Make a Difference: How Should They Be Counted?

raw_comment:
Headline- U.S. Dominates Olympic Medal Count Once Again, Other Countries Who Are Catching Up
1. This graph shows how countries are ranked based on their Olympic medal counts, with different values given to gold, silver, and bronze medals. What I first noticed was how the United States is clearly in first place because of its large number of gold medals, while China comes in second. Countries like Britain and France are also ranked, but their positions change depending on how the medals are counted. I also noticed that as the ranking decreased, so did the colors. For example, the US, is a dark red, and China is still red, but it’s much lighter than the US, and then gradually the colors begin to go down the color scale or the rainbow. I interpret the different places/numbers inside the boxes to be what place the country consistently placed in.
2. I wonder why the U.S. focuses so much on gold medals compared to other countries. I also wonder what all the lines and different sections of each box mean. For example, why is Jamaica split up all over the place, but is one color? While Brazil is less split up, but has multiple different colors. 
3. This relates to my community because many people here love watching the Olympics. The Olympics seem to bring out a very patriotic spirit in everyone in my community, especially when it comes to winning. We are often separated, but when it comes to the Olympics, everyone in my community comes together.

raw_comment:
1. I noticed that each box represents the amount of Olympic medals each country earned in the summer Olympics. The USA landed in first with the most amount of medals overall, even though China earned an equal amount of gold medals. In Britain, Canada, and France, it shows the countries' positions if gold medals were valued overall instead of all medals being valued equally. 
2. I wonder why this graph skips from France, which ended in 3-5 place, to Canada, which finished in 11- 12 place. What is the reason for this gap? Why is Britain placed before France if Britain is in 3-7 place, ending at a lower number than France? How can a country be in multiple places at once? Were some countries not included because they lacked popularity/interest?
3. As an American, the USA's coming out on top in the Olympics has increased patriotism and pride in my community. Even those Americans who believe their country is imperfect have become patriotic after this win. However, it has also increased hateful speech directed toward athletes from other countries. 
4. "Go For the Bronze! It Counts Just as Much..."

|---|---|---|

| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

I noticed that by increasing the value of gold compared to the others, it had an inconsistent effect across the countries. For example, countries like Brazil go down in rankings when the value of gold increases. However, countries such as Kenya do better when the value of gold is increased. This shows that there is no real correlation between the value of gold and how countries are ranked

What do you wonder?
Why countries such as Norway and Jamaica have so many different rankings on their graph compared to countries such as Canada/

How does this relate to your community?
This relates to my community as it shows how dominant the US is in world athletics. Being from the US, US dominance brings a sense of patriotism to citizens.

sentence_classifications.image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I noticed that the color red represents 1st place, and moving down to blue becomes the worst ranked. When looking at the possible outcomes, a lot of things change when you take into consideration how much each medal is valued/accounted for. For example, looking at Britain, France and Canada, if medals were counted equally, they would all be sitting in a higher positioned rank. In contrast, when looking at Norway, if all medals were valued equally, they would be in 26th, but if gold medals were the only thing taken into account, they would be in 18th.

What do you wonder?
I wonder how the scoring system will change over the years. Some people may have an opinion strong enough to persuade a change. Maybe more technology will be used when ranking the teams, to have a balance of everything. 

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to me because I watch the Olympics, so however the scoring works determines who I see win. This also affects the community because the U.S. competes in the Olympics, and living here, that is a community that we are all part of.

I noticed that the United States and China won the same amount of gold medals, but because the US won more silver medals they ended up winning the most overall. I also noticed that passed China, all other countries’ placing is in between a certain amount of numbers (take Kenya being in “16-21 place”).
I wonder why people debate how much gold medals should be worth overall. I think maybe the teams are just annoyed that they lost and realize if all medals were worth the same then they could climb higher on the ranks. I also wonder why most English-speaking countries got in the top 20 (besides China, of course).
This relates to my community because it brings America together in celebration. We were first overall which makes Americans feel a sense of pride towards our athletes. It also brings people closer together because most of us can agree that we want to win the Olympics. It may also bring resentment towards people from competing countries who argue they should have won instead.

raw_comment:
Notices?
I noticed that there were lots of numbers and big boxes displaying unique countries’ data. I also seemed to notice that the more populous countries were closer to the top of the graph, displaying the lower numbered placements.
Wonders?
I wondered what particularly the graph was showing, as there are many confusing lines and numbers all over the place. I also wondered why some countries have varying shades of their color, whereas America/China had the same shade of red for its entire box of Jamaica with the same shade of blue. Lastly, I wonder why each country values the medals uniquely? Why is it that some medals are worth more, less, or the same to one country versus another?
Relationship to Community?

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.
raw_comment:
What do you notice? I noticed that when they weigh the medals differently, many of the countries tend to move down in ranking. The fewer amount of medals a country has caused it to move down at a more drastic rate than the countries with more medals overall. When the medals are weighted the same, the countries all have a higher rating. The United States and China both remained at the top two options. 


What do you wonder? I wonder how the ranking of the different countries will change over time and if one country will transcend above the rest. 


How does this relate to you and your community? This graph relates to me because I watch the olympics and follow the athletes. Many of the Olympic athletes also play on my favorite sports teams. This connects my community because many people in the community watch their favorite sports in the Olympics.

raw_comment:

I wonder how they decided how many points each medal is worth and why that medal corresponds to that placement. I also wonder what country would have the greatest change in placement if all medals were ruled the same.
This relates to me and my community because the olympics is something that brings all Americans together to cheer and root for each other, because at the end of the day we are still on that team in a way.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.
raw_comment:
I notice that no matter what value is placed on the different medals the United States is first and China is second. I also noticed that the further down the leaderboard the more place changes there are with the new rules. Jamaica has the biggest leap of 13 whole places if the values were changed.

I wonder how the National Olympic Committee scores countries in the Olympics. I also wonder if they will change the scoring to medals per capita like some people have talked about. Why do the places change more the further down the list you go?

I live in the United States so seeing the U.S. be number one no matter what gives me a sense of pride in my country. People in the U.S. all unite together to support the athletes that represent us so I felt a strong sense of community seeing the U.S. win.

image_description:
1. **Chart type**:  
   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.
raw_comment:
-I noticed that the graph has information regarding the medals each country won, and their placement in comparison to other countries by using different systems of weighting Olympic medals for scoring. As you go down the rankings, there are far more possible placements, as they have fewer medals, meaning the different weighting affects these countries more. 

-I wonder about the real application of the graph, as mentioned, that there are comparable graphs of other countries as well as the Refugee Olympic Team. Alongside this, I would like to see a breakdown of sports, and would need more background information regarding facilities and the countries that usually perform well in the Olympic games. 

-This relates to my community as the Olympic Games are a world-wide event, and many people watch to support their country - including me. 

-“Meddling with Olympic Medals: How Does the Podium Change?”

raw_comment:
I notice that the US and China have little diversity in medal distribution regardless of how many were rewarded. They both took 1st and 2nd for having the most amount of medals and it didn’t matter much what worth each medal was. As countries have less and less medals, their placement has much more variety. Giving a 3-2-1 value to each medal in the order of gold-silver-bronze is what I notice as the best way to count and value medals.

I wonder how this was calculated and graphed because at first it seems very hard to read and to comprehend. I also wonder how this might be simplified for those who have difficulty reading out-of-the-ordinary graphs.

We can use the graph set up to count/measure objects in our own area and rank them based on the value of their placement given. Such objects may include groceries, toys, arsenal, ect. We can also use this data to extrapolate what might be the predicted medal count for the upcoming Olympic games.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the US and China have a completely solid color, whereas all the other countries have some variation. I also noticed that Jamaica and Norway could be a number of different ranks, even though they’re at the bottom. I wonder why the lower ranking countries have so many different possible rankings. I also wonder which way of choosing a winner would be the most fair, and how we’ve done it in the past. This relates to me and my community because so many people (including myself) watch the Olympics, so it’s very important to have a standardized way to rank the winners. Even though we already know that the US would be in the same spot no matter what, it’s important to see how the other countries line up.
 Headline: Does Being a Gold Digger Pay Out? Weighing How to Rank Olympic Teams

raw_comment:
I noticed that the US is in first place with a darker red, claiming that it has won over China being second. As the places decrease, the colors fade into lighter hues of orange and yellow. The US and China were only ones with a solid color in the whole graph while other countries had more diversity with shades and color schemes. 

I wonder what the meaning of the colors are, why is red the most prominent for the winning countries? Why are the lines shaped how they are and what do they mean? 

This impacts the community as it shows the difference in how people value the medals at the olympics. Some may say bronze is just as good of an achievement as gold or, others may claim that bronze is not worth anything.

#1: I noticed that as the ranking decreased, so did the colors. For example, the number one, is a dark red, and the second ranked, was still red, but a much lighter red than the first one, and the third ranked, is even lighter than the second ranked, and gradually the colors begin to go down the color scale. #3: This relates to me and my community because some athletes are looking to get as high as being in the Olympics one day. 
#4: The Medal Dominance: US Ranks Number One After Close Call with China.

|---|---|---|

| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

3. **Data variables**:

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |
| Relative value of silver vs. bronze medals | Quantitative | Position on x-axis |
| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

raw_comment:
I noticed that the US has the most medals won but China has the higher ratio of first place gold medalists then second or third place. If they went just based on gold medals won, the US and China would be tied but measuring silver and copper as well makes the US win.
I wonder how the graph would change if they just measured gold medals or if they measured the highest ratio of gold medals to silver or copper.
I'm from the US and am friends with someone who is very patriotic during the Olympics but I don't care too much about it. While I don't care, a majority of people do. They go crazy when their team makes first and get less happy when they get second or third. 
Title: Measure of the Most Important Medals.

raw_comment:
1. I notice that the graph creates a pyramidal shape, or a hierarchical scale. With the top being it's proclaimed winner, this is expressed by having it be the largest cube, followed by the others who fell short of first having progressively smaller cubes. This structure implies dominance from the United States, and creates the sense that we won by so much, when that may not have been the case. 
2. I wonder why there is so much variability in the countries scores on the bottom rung? It feels like there should be a standard indicating how much Medals are worth, so the outcome is more clear. I think this would add to the competitive nature of the Olympics and only fuel overall competition.
3. For me and my community, I have seen a lot of pride in the United States's performance in the Olympics. It provides something to come together on when I feel we are at a time where the divide is emphasized rather than the unity of our people. Gathering around the television and watching our country compete helps us forget about differences, and show us what makes us a nation.
4. "Majority of Medals Mark the Monarchs"

   A **faceted rank-region heatmap / partition-style chart** showing possible Olympic medal-count ranks under different medal-weighting schemes.

2. **Layout techniques**:  
   - **Small multiples / faceting by country**: each panel represents one country.
   - Within each panel, the space is **partitioned into colored regions** corresponding to possible rank outcomes.
   - **Color** encodes rank level on a continuous scale (from 1st to 25th or lower).
   - Some panels include **text labels** inside regions and **small circular markers** near the title indicating medal counts.

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Country | Categorical/nominal | Faceting into separate panels; panel title/label |

| Relative value of gold vs. silver medals | Quantitative | Position on y-axis |
| Possible rank in medal count | Ordinal | Color/hue of regions; text labels inside regions |
| Gold medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small colored circle near panel title |
| Silver medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small gray circle near panel title |
| Bronze medal count | Quantitative | Numeric label in small bronze-colored circle near panel title |

Visible annotations/axis notes clarify the weighting dimensions (e.g., “All medals valued equally,” “Only care about gold medals,” “Gold worth 20x silver,” “Silver worth 20x bronze”), but these are explanatory labels rather than additional data variables.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
I notice multiple things on these graphs, the first being that both the U.S. and China are firmly glued in their standings, for whatever way the medals are counted, it does not matter and the only places they are capable of getting are first and second. I also noticed that their are no clear ways of saying which medal is worth another, and it is basically just up to interpretation.

What do you wonder?
How would medals per Capita affect these results?

How does this relate to you and your community?
In my community, people are greatly affected. An example being; people who otherwise complain about our country (USA) become patriotic and devoted to the athletes. The Olympics sparks joy in people, and our success in them is even more riveting.

Create a catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea.

Olympic Ores And The Objective Value They Hold.

Based on these graphs, I notice that they rank them in many ways. The U.S. has the most medals in total. We are also tied with China for most Golds. Therefore, we are ranked no.1 either way if you rank us by medal count or by most gold medals.

This relates with me and my community since a diver from Wantagh went to the Olympics seeking a gold medal. This shows me how rare it is to get gold or any medal for yourself and the country. 

A catchy Headline that would capture the graph’s main idea would be “The Countries and their Strong, Fast, and Winners."
